title: Manipulation Technique Compendium
scope: Defensive detection taxonomy for persuasion, dark patterns, gaming monetization, social media influence operations, and PsyOps-style communication analysis.
safety_boundary: This compendium supports detection, audit, tagging, and risk scoring. It does not provide operational guidance for exploiting audiences or improving manipulative campaigns.

techniques.name: Scarcity and urgency pressure
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Loss aversion and time pressure reduce deliberation and make the user overweight the cost of missing out.

examples.description: Countdowns, low-stock claims, expiring discounts, and limited-time offers.
Seasonal skins, rotating stores, event passes, and expiring gacha banners.
Messages implying the opportunity is rare, immediate, or available only to a small number of respondents.

citations: FTC 2022 Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

techniques.name: Social proof and manufactured consensus
techniques.psychological_mechanism: People infer safety, truth, or value from apparent popularity, especially under uncertainty.

examples.description: Artificial likes, comments, shares, hashtag pushes, and comment brigading.
Popularity counters, fake testimonials, and bestseller claims.
Coordinated inauthentic behavior makes a narrative appear organically popular.

techniques.name: Authority and credibility laundering
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Authority cues transfer trust from institutions, experts, local identities, or news-like formats to the message.

examples.description: Use of professional titles, implied guarantees, or institutional-looking presentation.
Fake media brands, impersonated locals, and personas presenting claims as independent reporting.
Appeals to authority without verifiable source support.

techniques.name: Reciprocity and obligation creation
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Receiving a gift, favor, or apparent concession creates felt obligation to reciprocate or comply.

examples.description: Free samples, bonuses, and gifts followed by an ask.
Personalized favors, attention, or support used to create relational debt.
Financial help framed as generosity may create pressure for future compliance.

citations: FTC 2022 Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

techniques.name: Commitment, consistency, and foot-in-the-door
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Small initial commitments increase later compliance because people prefer to act consistently with prior choices.

examples.description: Small free trials or low-friction signups followed by larger commitments.
Polls, pledges, quizzes, and identity labels that make later action feel consistent.
Requests to first respond privately or answer a small personal question before larger asks.

techniques.name: Obstruction and friction asymmetry
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Provider-preferred actions are made easier than protective actions, exploiting inertia, fatigue, and cognitive load.

examples.description: Easy subscription with hard cancellation or refund process.
Accept-all consent is prominent while reject or customize paths are buried.
One-click purchases paired with hidden refund or spending-control flows.

techniques.name: Forced action and unrelated disclosure
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Access is conditioned on accepting an unrelated action, creating coercive choice architecture.

examples.description: Registration required before viewing material price or availability.
Consent walls that lack an equivalent reject path.
Account or contact-sharing prompts required for unrelated functionality.

citations: FTC 2022 Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

techniques.name: Interface interference and visual steering
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Visual salience, defaults, labels, placement, and contrast steer choices without changing nominal options.

examples.description: Bright primary purchase buttons and muted decline links.
Preselected tracking options or unequal consent choices.
Store prompts with dominant purchase paths and weak confirmation controls.

techniques.name: Sneaking, hidden costs, and drip pricing
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Material terms are delayed or obscured after commitment momentum has formed, exploiting sunk-cost and anchoring effects.

examples.description: Fees added late in checkout after an attractive headline price.
Trial or renewal terms made less salient than the immediate benefit.
Real-money cost obscured through currency bundles and leftover balances.

citations: FTC 2022 Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

techniques.name: Confirmshaming and guilt pressure
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Shame, guilt, or fear of negative self-image is attached to refusal, making rejection psychologically costly.

examples.description: Decline buttons framed as irresponsible, boring, or foolish.
Prompts that imply the user is neglecting friends, safety, or status if they decline.
Emotional claims that make refusal feel cruel or ungrateful.

citations: FTC 2022 Bringing Dark Patterns to Light

techniques.name: Randomized monetization and variable rewards
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Variable-ratio rewards and rare outcomes encourage repeated spending and resemble gambling reinforcement schedules.

examples.description: Loot boxes, card packs, crates, gacha pulls, rarity tiers, and audiovisual win effects.
High-frequency markets and rapid bet settlement compress reflection time.
Chance-based rewards paired with limited events and purchasable currency.

techniques.name: Gacha escalation and pity-progress framing
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Progress counters, rotating prize pools, and limited characters make continued spending feel like rational progress toward an otherwise scarce reward.

examples.description: Pity counters, step-up summons, guaranteed-after-N banners, and limited character pools.
Non-even currency bundles create leftover balances and encourage repeat purchase.
Regulators scrutinize misleading odds, costs, and child-directed purchase design.

techniques.name: Coordinated inauthentic behavior
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Hidden coordination manufactures consensus and manipulates both human trust and platform ranking systems.

examples.description: Networks of accounts synchronize posts, links, hashtags, and mutual amplification.
Astroturfed support or opposition presented as grassroots sentiment.
Cross-platform persona networks obscure the actor behind a narrative.

techniques.name: Flooding and firehose communication
techniques.psychological_mechanism: High-volume, repetitive, multichannel claims exploit familiarity bias, attention exhaustion, and correction resistance.

examples.description: Rapid repetition of inconsistent claims across many outlets and accounts.
Floods of comments or posts that overwhelm opposing information.
Narratives that persist through volume even when factually corrected.

techniques.name: Emotional and identity targeting
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Messages tied to fear, status, belonging, humiliation, pride, or grievance activate motivated reasoning and social identity defense.

examples.description: Wedge narratives amplify group threat, distrust, and polarization.
Identity-based appeals make a purchase feel like self-expression or status protection.
Financial support, independence, safety, or family obligation can function as vulnerability multipliers.

techniques.name: Narrative laundering and cross-platform recycling
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Claims are moved across personas, platforms, pseudo-media, influencers, and communities until origin and coordination become hard to see.

examples.description: A claim seeded by a fake account is reposted by pages, websites, and influencers.
Fake outlets and personas create apparent independent corroboration.
Dubious claims are introduced as already-reported facts without provenance.

techniques.name: Fake Urgency / Baseless Countdown Timer
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Exploits scarcity heuristic and loss aversion; creates false time pressure to bypass deliberation. Often baseless (no real limit).

examples.description: Limited-time offers or countdowns on e-commerce checkout.
Limited-time events or sales with timers.
False 'limited time' or 'act now' in investment/scam ads or marketplace listings.
'Sólo por pocas horas' or timers in e-comm (SERNAC Chile notes in 64% sampled sites).

triggers: Time-sensitive decisions, uncertainty, mobile/fast-scroll contexts; loss aversion bias.
language_patterns: Últimas unidades / sólo por pocas horas
citations: Gray et al. (2024) ontology (Urgency category); SERNAC Chile (2021); FTC (2022)

techniques.name: Fake Scarcity / False Low Stock or High Demand Messages
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Leverages scarcity principle and FOMO; implies limited availability or popularity to increase perceived value, even when fabricated.

examples.description: 'Only 2 left!' or 'X people viewing' on product pages.
'Few available' or demand claims in used-goods listings or limited-investment pitches.
SERNAC Chile: 'últimas unidades' signals in Chilean e-comm.

triggers: Product choice under uncertainty; social comparison; status quo or bandwagon bias.
citations: Gray et al. (2024) ontology (Scarcity); Mathur et al. (2019); SERNAC (2021)

techniques.name: Fake Social Proof / Deceptive Testimonials or Activity Messages
techniques.psychological_mechanism: Exploits conformity and social proof heuristics; fabricated reviews, 'X bought this', or pop-up activity to normalize action.

examples.description: Fake reviews or 'Most popular' badges.
Doubtful testimonials or 'X people viewing/bought' pop-ups in listings or financial products.
SERNAC Chile notes activity notifications and 'testimonios dudosos' in e-comm and financial cases.

triggers: Uncertainty or social validation needs; bandwagon effect.
language_patterns: X people have bought this today!

covered_categories: Gaming monetization and betting-app pressure mechanics
Social media and political influence operations
weak_domains: Debate-specific manipulative rhetoric needs a deeper argumentative fallacy and conversational coercion pass.
Spanish-language and Peru-specific examples improved via agentic fan-out but still need more direct ad corpus from Phase 4.
Quantitative prevalence estimates outside e-commerce and gaming remain uneven.
emerged_families: Autonomy erosion through friction asymmetry and interface steering
Monetized uncertainty through randomized rewards and obfuscated currency
Manufactured consensus through coordinated inauthentic behavior
Vulnerability multipliers that intensify otherwise general persuasion patterns
LatAm/Spanish urgency-scarcity and activity signals in consumer/classified contexts (SERNAC-aligned)
what_worked: Parallel sub-agents produced strong domain slices for regulator/HCI, gaming, and influence operations.

Agentic fan-out Round 4 added post-2018 ontology (Gray), SERNAC Chile LatAm examples (urgency, scarcity, social proof, preselection), AI extensions, and classified-adjacent patterns with Spanish language triggers.
The three-round STORM structure separated foundational sources, domain applications, and fan-out synthesis.
The compendium format is directly usable for later annotation and model-label schemas.
what_failed_or_needs_improvement: Phase 1 is broad; later passes should add more Spanish-language sources and Latin American case studies.
Several gaming and influence-operation findings are correlational or campaign-specific, so model labels should avoid overclaiming causality.
The compendium needs Phase 2 context before weighting Peru-specific vulnerability multipliers.
next_phase_strategy: Use official Peru statistics, UN/World Bank/ILO/INEI/MIMP sources, and academic studies before any lower-quality media sources.
Segment young and young-adult women by urban/semi-urban context where evidence allows.
Map each multiplier to Phase 1 techniques without creating exploitative message recipes.
